lessonTitle: Bacterial Cell Structure: Wall, Capsule, Pili and Gene Transfer

blocks.text: A 70-year-old woman with a splenectomy years ago arrives febrile and drowsy; blood cultures grow Gram-positive diplococci with a thick polysaccharide coat that her phagocytes cannot grip. The same bacterial surface that Gram stain reveals, antibiotics attack and the immune system struggles to recognise is the subject of this unit.

blocks.markdown: Bacteria are **prokaryotes**: they have no nucleus, one circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes. Almost everything clinically important about them sits **outside** the cytoplasmic membrane. The cell envelope decides how a bacterium stains, which antibiotics reach it, whether it survives phagocytosis, how it sticks to tissue and how it releases toxins. We then ask a second question: once a bacterium has a useful gene (for a toxin or for resistance), how is it passed to another bacterium?

blocks.title: Peptidoglycan
blocks.text: Peptidoglycan (murein) is a mesh polymer of alternating N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) sugars, cross-linked by short peptide bridges. It forms a rigid, bag-like layer around the cell that resists osmotic lysis. Human cells do not make it, which is why many antibiotics that block its synthesis are selectively toxic.

blocks.markdown: **Gram-positive** bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer (many stacked sheets) outside the cytoplasmic membrane. Threaded through it are **teichoic acids** and lipoteichoic acids, which anchor the wall and are immunostimulatory. **Gram-negative** bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched in the **periplasmic space** between the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane and an **outer membrane**. The outer leaflet of that outer membrane is **lipopolysaccharide (LPS)**, whose lipid A portion is the endotoxin. Water-filled **porin** channels let small hydrophilic molecules cross the outer membrane, and also limit entry of some antibiotics.

blocks.caption: Cell wall comparison
rows: Loses crystal violet, takes counterstain: pink/red
Prominent; contains beta-lactamases in many species

blocks.title: Predicting a stain and a consequence
blocks.prompt: A clinical isolate has a wall with a very thin peptidoglycan layer, an outer membrane bearing lipid A, and no teichoic acids. Predict its Gram reaction and one consequence of its wall structure.

steps.text: Identify the key structures. A thin peptidoglycan layer with an outer membrane is the Gram-negative architecture.

Link to the stain. The decolouriser (alcohol or acetone) dissolves the outer membrane lipid and the thin peptidoglycan cannot retain the crystal violet-iodine complex, so the cell is decolourised and then takes up the pink counterstain (safranin).
Link to function. Lipid A in the outer membrane is endotoxin, so lysis of these cells can release a potent inflammatory stimulus. The outer membrane also restricts some large or hydrophobic drugs.

blocks.answer: Gram-negative (pink/red); consequences include endotoxin release and reduced permeability to some antibiotics.

blocks.markdown: **Capsule.** Many bacteria are surrounded by a loose, gel-like layer, usually polysaccharide (poly-D-glutamate in *Bacillus anthracis*). The capsule is **antiphagocytic**: it masks surface structures and hinders complement deposition (opsonisation) so neutrophils and macrophages cannot ingest the organism efficiently. Encapsulated organisms such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* type b and *Neisseria meningitidis* are classic causes of invasive disease, and the antibodies and opsonins needed to clear them are made after vaccination against the capsule. Patients without a functioning spleen, which clears opsonised encapsulated bacteria, are particularly vulnerable.

**Pili (fimbriae)** are thin protein filaments. Their tips carry **adhesins** that bind specific host receptors, allowing colonisation of mucosa and resisting flushing, for example type 1 and P pili of uropathogenic *E. coli* in the urinary tract. A special **sex pilus** (conjugative pilus) joins a donor to a recipient bacterium for conjugation. **Flagella** are different: they are long, helical motility organs, not adhesive.

blocks.caption: Surface structures and their roles in virulence
rows: Adhesion to host cells; some enable gene transfer
Conjugation bridge between donor and recipient

blocks.markdown: **Genetic elements.** The chromosome carries essential genes. **Plasmids** are small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecules that replicate independently and often carry non-essential but advantageous genes such as antibiotic resistance. Bacteria exchange DNA by **horizontal gene transfer** by three routes: **transformation** (uptake of free DNA from the environment), **transduction** (DNA carried by a bacteriophage) and **conjugation** (direct cell-to-cell transfer through a sex pilus, usually of a plasmid). A **bacteriophage** is a virus that infects bacteria. In the **lytic cycle** it replicates, lyses the host and releases progeny; the number released per infected cell is the **burst size**. In the **lysogenic cycle** the phage genome integrates as a prophage and is replicated with the chromosome, sometimes encoding toxins (for example diphtheria toxin, via a prophage).

blocks.title: Quantifying a conjugation experiment
blocks.prompt: Donor *E. coli* carrying a resistance plasmid are mixed with 5.0 x 10^7 plasmid-free recipients. Afterwards, 2.5 x 10^3 recipients are found to have acquired resistance. Express the conjugation frequency as transconjugants per 10^6 recipients.

steps.text: Define the quantity. Frequency = transconjugants divided by recipients.
Compute: f = 5.0 x 10^-5 transconjugants per recipient.
Rescale to per 10^6 recipients by multiplying by 10^6: 5.0 x 10^-5 x 10^6 = 50.

items: Transformation: naked DNA is taken up by a competent cell, with no phage and no cell contact.
Transduction: a phage accidentally packages bacterial DNA (generalised) or carries adjacent genes after prophage excision (specialised) and delivers it to the next host.
Conjugation: a donor with a conjugative plasmid forms a sex pilus and transfers a plasmid copy to a recipient.
Lysogenic conversion: a prophage gives its host a new property such as toxin production.

blocks.title: Why the envelope and plasmids matter clinically
blocks.text: Wall structure predicts stain, antibiotic access and endotoxin. Capsules explain failure of phagocytosis and the special risk of asplenia. Plasmids and phages explain how resistance and toxin genes jump between species within a hospital in a short time.

blocks.title: Common confusions
blocks.text: Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane and no LPS, but they are not immune to cell wall antibiotics: their thick peptidoglycan is exactly the target. Pili adhere; flagella move. Transduction needs a phage vector; conjugation needs direct cell contact.

points: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids, no outer membrane. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan, periplasm and outer membrane carrying LPS (endotoxin).
Capsules resist phagocytosis; pili mediate adhesion and sex pili mediate conjugation.
Plasmids carry accessory genes; transformation, transduction and conjugation spread them horizontally.
Lytic phages lyse host cells; lysogenic phages integrate and may encode toxins.

questions.stem: Which structure is found in the Gram-negative cell envelope but not in Gram-positive bacteria?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the outer membrane with LPS is characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria.
distractorRationale.b: Thick peptidoglycan is a Gram-positive feature.
distractorRationale.c: Teichoic and lipoteichoic acids are Gram-positive features.
distractorRationale.d: All bacteria have a cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an additional outer membrane whose outer leaflet is LPS. Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane but a thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acids.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is treated for a Gram-negative bacteraemia and develops a transient rise in fever and fall in blood pressure shortly after antibiotics lyse many bacteria. Which cell envelope component best explains this?

options.text: Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane
Teichoic acid in the peptidoglycan layer

questions.correctOptionText: Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lipid A is the endotoxin released when Gram-negative cells lyse.
distractorRationale.b: Teichoic acids belong to Gram-positive walls, not Gram-negative organisms.
distractorRationale.c: Flagellin drives motility and can stimulate immunity but is not the classic endotoxin.
distractorRationale.d: Capsule resists phagocytosis; it is not the main cause of endotoxic fever and hypotension.

questions.explanation: Lipid A is the bioactive portion of LPS and triggers cytokine release through host pattern recognition receptors. Lysing Gram-negative bacteria releases more of it, which can transiently worsen the inflammatory response.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child has had his spleen removed after trauma. Why is he at special risk from encapsulated bacteria?

options.text: Capsules resist phagocytosis, and the spleen is the main site for clearing opsonised encapsulated bacteria
Capsules make bacteria motile, and the spleen normally traps motile cells
Capsules are toxins that the spleen normally neutralises
Capsules transfer resistance genes, which the spleen normally destroys

questions.correctOptionText: Capsules resist phagocytosis, and the spleen is the main site for clearing opsonised encapsulated bacteria

distractorRationale.b: Motility is a function of flagella, not capsules.
distractorRationale.c: Capsules are not toxins; they protect against phagocytosis.
distractorRationale.d: Gene transfer is mediated by plasmids, phages and DNA uptake, not capsules.

questions.explanation: Encapsulated organisms evade phagocytosis unless coated with antibody and complement. The spleen filters blood and removes opsonised bacteria, so asplenic patients need vaccination against organisms such as pneumococcus.

questions.stem: Which surface structure allows uropathogenic Escherichia coli to attach to bladder epithelium and resist being flushed out by urine flow?

distractorRationale.b: Flagella move cells but do not anchor them to receptors.
distractorRationale.c: Peptidoglycan gives structural strength, not specific adhesion.
distractorRationale.d: Plasmids may encode adhesins but DNA itself does not bind epithelium.

questions.explanation: Pilin tips carry adhesins that bind receptors on urothelial cells. This lets the bacterium colonise the urinary tract despite the shear of flowing urine.

questions.stem: A non-toxigenic strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae acquires the ability to make diphtheria toxin after infection with a temperate phage that integrates its genome into the bacterial chromosome. Which process is this?

options.text: Uptake of free DNA by transformation
Lytic phage replication with immediate cell lysis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the integrated phage encodes the toxin gene.
distractorRationale.b: No cell-to-cell pilus contact is described.
distractorRationale.c: The DNA arrives in a phage, not as free DNA.
distractorRationale.d: Lytic replication kills the host; here the phage integrates and the host survives.

questions.explanation: In the lysogenic cycle the phage genome is integrated as a prophage and replicated with the chromosome. Genes it carries, such as a toxin gene, are expressed by the host, a phenomenon called lysogenic conversion.

questions.stem: In a conjugation experiment, 8.0 x 10^7 plasmid-free recipient cells are mixed with donors. Afterwards 1.6 x 10^3 recipients are found to carry the resistance plasmid. Calculate the conjugation frequency as the number of transconjugants per 10^6 recipient cells. Give your answer in transconjugants per 10^6 recipients.
questions.explanation: Frequency per recipient = 1.6 x 10^3 / 8.0 x 10^7 = 2.0 x 10^-5. Multiplying by 10^6 gives 20 transconjugants per 10^6 recipients.

questions.stem: A single lytic bacteriophage infects one bacterial cell. Each infected cell lyses and releases a burst size of 120 phages, and every progeny phage then infects a fresh cell and does the same. Assuming no losses, how many phage particles are released in total at the end of the third lytic cycle (the third round of lysis)? Give your answer as a number of phage particles.
questions.explanation: Each cycle multiplies the phage number by the burst size: after one cycle 120, after two 120^2 = 14 400, after three 120^3 = 1 728 000. This exponential amplification explains why lytic phage can clear a bacterial culture quickly.

questions.stem: Compare the cell walls of a Gram-positive and a Gram-negative bacterium and explain how the difference leads to their different Gram stain results and different consequences for infection.
markingGuide: Gram-positive: thick, multilayered peptidoglycan with teichoic/lipoteichoic acids, no outer membrane
Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan in the periplasm, plus an outer membrane with LPS and porins
Gram-positive retains crystal violet-iodine and stains purple after decolouriser
Gram-negative is decolourised (outer membrane damaged, thin peptidoglycan) and stains pink with counterstain
Gram-negative lipid A acts as endotoxin and the outer membrane limits entry of some antibiotics
questions.explanation: A good answer links structure to the stain and to clinical behaviour. The outer membrane and LPS give Gram-negative organisms endotoxin activity and reduced permeability, while the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positive organisms retains the dye.

questions.stem: Explain how a polysaccharide capsule and surface pili each contribute to the ability of a bacterium to cause disease.
markingGuide: Capsule is antiphagocytic: masks surface structures and impairs opsonisation by complement and antibody
Examples of encapsulated pathogens (such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis)
Pili carry adhesins that bind host cell receptors and allow colonisation and resistance to flushing
Example of adhesion by pili (such as E. coli in the urinary tract)
Sex pili may also mediate conjugation and spread of virulence or resistance genes
questions.explanation: The capsule helps the organism survive in blood by evading phagocytes, whereas pili help it attach and colonise. Together they help explain how organisms establish and sustain infection.

questions.stem: Describe how a plasmid and a bacteriophage can each transfer genes from one bacterium to another. Name the process in each case and state one clinical consequence.
markingGuide: Plasmid: circular extrachromosomal DNA transferred by conjugation via a sex pilus from donor to recipient
Conjugation requires direct cell contact; plasmid usually copied so the donor keeps it
Bacteriophage: transduction, in which phage packages bacterial DNA (generalised) or carries adjacent genes (specialised) to a new host
Lysogenic conversion: prophage encoding a toxin gene gives a new property
Clinical consequence such as spread of antibiotic resistance or toxin production (for example diphtheria toxin) between bacteria
questions.explanation: Conjugation uses a plasmid and a sex pilus, while transduction uses a phage as a vector. Both are forms of horizontal gene transfer that let resistance and virulence genes move between strains.
